summary: Part 3 of the legacy manuscript (book.md lines 5883-9479, about 37,000 words) covers the application and advanced chapters and all back matter. Ch. 17 is black holes (Schwarzschild derivation, Eddington-Finkelstein, infall and hovering, ISCO and photon sphere, a Kerr orientation, a TOV star, photon/observer frequency). Ch. 18 is gravitational waves (linearization, gauge and TT reduction, detector response, quadrupole formula with a full 1/5 angular-average derivation, binary chirp, GW150914). Ch. 19 is cosmology (FLRW curvature, Friedmann and continuity equations, power-law solutions, redshift, conformal time, three horizons, Ricci-vs-Weyl comparison, distance measures, Oppenheimer-Snyder dust collapse). Ch. 20 is 3+1/ADM (lapse and shift, extrinsic curvature, Gauss-Codazzi constraints, Friedmann as a constraint, phase-space degree-of-freedom count, an Euler/RK4 constraint-residual lab, the hole argument). Ch. 21 is tetrads and Cartan forms (polar plane vs sphere, a surface-of-revolution exercise, gauge analogy, spinors, torsion/nonmetricity, Palatini). Ch. 22 is focusing and black-hole thermodynamics (Raychaudhuri, energy conditions, trapped surfaces and Penrose's theorem, Cauchy horizons, Euclidean Hawking temperature, entropy, area theorem, Kerr first law, information/Page curve). Ch. 23 is GR as an effective field theory (power counting, nonrenormalizability, spin-2 self-coupling, Lovelock, the cosmological-constant problem, semiclassical gravity, what tests constrain). Ch. 24 is a synthesis (a Rindler metric-to-measurement check, a 10-step calculation checklist, four calibration geometries, on-shell vs off-shell). The back matter is Appendix A (30 solved exercises spanning the whole book), B (formula sheet), C (glossary), D (reading list and 35 cited sources) and E (index checklist plus three misconception problems). guides.json entries 17-24 give each chapter a question, payoff, takeaway and check/answer. Four calculated labs are embedded here: star (§17.8), photon (§17.9), distances (§19.11) and evolution (§20.7). Their models are small pure functions in web/relativity-models.js, validated against independent analytic limits in scripts/check-relativity-models.mjs. Overall the science is unusually careful and nearly fault-free on spot-check: the derivations are complete, every result states its assumptions, and imported results (Kerr metric, first-class constraint algebra, spin structure, Hawking flux) are flagged as imported. It makes excellent grounding for the vault and the tutor. As novice teaching it is dense and caveat-heavy, and equations come before visuals (docs/visual-development-plan-2026-09-09.md: 27 displayed equation blocks precede the first visual in Ch. 18, 38 in Ch. 21). Practice is segregated in Appendix A. Chapters 20-23 were an 'optional deeper trail' outside the core route. Known content gaps: Kerr depth, no Reissner-Nordstrom at all (zero mentions), and no Schwarzschild or collapse causal diagram in book.md (the only conformal picture is the §19.8 cosmic-horizons figure; Kruskal maps live in a bridge lesson); antenna patterns, noise and real data for waves; density parameters and E(z) in the cosmology prose (they exist only inside the lab record); a solved inhomogeneous initial-data problem; Hodge duality and Maxwell in forms; a curved-spacetime capstone. Recommended use: reuse the derivation layers nearly verbatim; adapt chapters into short visual-first lessons; turn Appendix A/E and the guides into distributed, gradable practice; keep B/C/D as vault seeds.
lessons_learned: The most reusable thing in these chapters is the derivation-with-stated-assumptions style (e.g. §17.1 integrates d/dr[r(1-f)]=0 instead of announcing Schwarzschild; §18.7 derives the 1/5 by isotropic tensor averaging; §22.9 checks the Kerr first law algebraically). Import these as the derivation/deep layer of a lesson and as tutor grounding, not as the first thing a novice reads.

Caveat density is too high for primary novice text: almost every paragraph adds 'this does not mean...' or 'under the stated assumptions...'. grbook lessons should put one core claim per step up front and move qualifications into a collapsible 'fine print' or tutor-available layer, keeping the misconception checks as explicit quiz items.

Visuals arrived after the algebra (visual-development-plan: Ch. 18's first visual comes after 27 equation blocks, Ch. 21's after 38; build-site.mjs places pictures at section ends by policy). In grbook the experiment or diagram should open the lesson in plain language, with equations revealed progressively.

The four calculated labs set the right engineering pattern: a pure-function model shared by build time and browser (web/relativity-models.js), a declared record of units, assumptions, limitations and source (web/lab-records.js), and CI checks against independent analytic limits (the n=1 Lane-Emden radius sqrt(pi/2), dust and de Sitter comoving distances, photon reciprocity, RK4 convergence ratio between 12 and 20). Keep this model/record/check triad for every grbook demo.

A quantity must never live only inside a demo. The distances lab exposes Omega_m, Omega_Lambda, H0, E(z) and D_C = (c/H0) integral dz/E(z), but none appear in the Ch. 19 prose (grep finds no density parameter or critical density). Every control and readout needs a matching explanation in the lesson text.

Practice segregated into an appendix does not work (docs/learning-experience-audit.md: 'Practice is largely segregated from the moment a skill is acquired'). Appendix A solutions also sit inline in book.md with no reveal wrapper, unlike Appendix E's checkpoint details. Distribute exercises to the point of use, hide solutions behind attempts, and give answers a structured or numeric form an AI grader can check.

Review documents go stale fast. The 2026-09-09 comprehensive review says the course 'lacks ... the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation', but §17.8 and the star lab were added the same day (docs/course-evolution.md 'Recovered calculated laboratories'). Every review finding needs a date and a re-check before it drives work.

Stable IDs decoupled from titles saved links through retitling: content/section-ids.json still maps 18.5 to the old slug '18-5-retarded-solutions-the-field-receives-yesterday-s-news', and curriculum.mjs uses '19-5-solving-for-the-scale-factor-three-recognizable-cosmic-personalities'. grbook should key lessons and concepts to stable IDs from day one and treat headings as display text.

Symbol collisions multiply in late chapters: the curvature two-form is written with a calligraphic R in §21.4-21.8 but Omega in Appendix A.28 and the Cartan figure review; A is the normalized scale factor (§19, §20.7), horizon area (§22.7) and sphere radius (§24.4, A.8); omega is both spin connection (§21) and vorticity (§22); beta is both shift (§20) and velocity (§17.9). A per-lesson scoped symbol registry is needed; the legacy global tau heuristic already mislabeled a plotting time as proper time (review finding F01).

Advanced chapters need explicit prerequisite modules and a split between classical and semiclassical material. Ch. 22 had a dependency reversal at §22.7 (docs/novice-sequencing-audit-2026-09-09.md), and the core route in content/curriculum.mjs skips 20-23 entirely. Split focusing and the area theorem from Hawking radiation and information, and give each its own entry requirements.

A synthesis chapter built only on flat Rindler is too thin a capstone (comprehensive review row 24). grbook's final project should make the learner pick observers in a curved spacetime with matter (e.g. TOV exterior plus FLRW), compute, verify and predict a measurement.

Revision-log prose and small typos got past the automated checks: §19.11 says 'The worked example now obtains these distances', and §20.3 and §23.3 start a sentence lowercase after a bold lead-in ('extrinsic curvature need not...', 'if we truncate...'). Add prose linting and an editorial pass, not only math and link checks.

The guides.json pattern (one question, payoff, takeaway and check/answer per chapter) is a compact, high-value exit ticket that maps directly to a voice-tutor 'can you explain...' prompt. Keep it, but add several checks per lesson across predict/calculate/diagnose roles.

The late-added lab sections (§17.8 star, §17.9 photon, §20.7 evolution) already follow the order grbook wants: a physical picture in plain words, then the lab, then the derivation with an independent limiting check. They are the template for adapting the older equation-first sections, and §19.11 is the counter-example (derivation first, sliders for undefined Omega parameters after).

Keyword-derived topic tags are unreliable: a grep for 'Shapiro' in Part 3 only hits the BSSN acronym (Baumgarte, Shapiro, Shibata, Nakamura), yet §17.9 had been tagged 'Shapiro delay'. Tag concepts in the grbook vault only after a human or model reads the passage, and require a line reference for each tag.

Route status must come from one source. build-site.mjs hardcodes 'OPTIONAL DEEPER TRAIL' for chapters 20-23 while curriculum.mjs defines a horizons route that requires 21 and 22. grbook should derive every 'optional' or 'required' badge from the learner's chosen path in the registry.

A readout that can never change (the photon lab's 'locally measured light speed / c = 1') and a shared axis that flattens the key curve (D_A on a 0-50 Gpc axis) both hide the lesson the lab exists to teach. Review every demo's default state and ask whether the intended surprise is visible without reading numbers.

The QA screenshot default states contain exact, CI-verified numbers (photon 0.75593 = sqrt(4/7); star R=0.86584, M=0.15736 at rho_c=0.2, step 0.01; distances D_C=5179.9 Mpc at z=2). Carry them over as visual-regression and model-port fixtures so the Svelte ports can be checked against the legacy output.

assets.title: Chapter 17. Black holes: horizons, falling clocks, and orbits
assets.teaches: The learner derives the Schwarzschild exterior from a two-function spherical ansatz. They use the Kretschmann scalar 48m^2/r^6 to show r=2m is a chart failure and r=0 is not. They repair the chart with ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates and read the tilted future light cones. They compute a finite infall proper time (4m/3c from the horizon) against a diverging hovering acceleration. They find circular orbits and stability, separating 2m (horizon), 3m (photon sphere) and 6m (ISCO), and recover the Ch. 16 orbit equation. They learn the event horizon as a global causal boundary, meet the Kerr metric with ZAMO frame dragging, horizons and ergosurface, integrate a relativistic star with the TOV equation, and compare gravitational and Doppler frequency shifts between chosen observers.
assets.pedagogy: Opens with an operational question (can a light pulse escape from here?). Derivations are shown stepwise with commentary on where each term comes from (second derivative, Gamma-Gamma products, 2/r angular terms). It tests with invariants before interpreting the chart and contrasts two observer families (falling vs hovering). A summary table covers the three radii. §17.8 starts with a pressure-gradient slab intuition before the TOV equations. Collapsible 'Further calculation' details hold the Birkhoff time-dependence proof. Embedded star and photon labs each carry predict/observe prompts. Bridge lessons (horizon-directions, Kruskal causal map) are inserted at section ends by content/lesson-sequence.mjs.
assets.physics_model: Static spherical vacuum ansatz ds^2=-e^(2alpha)c^2dt^2+e^(2beta)dr^2+r^2dOmega^2, solved to f=1-2m/r with m=GM/c^2. EF metric -f c^2 dv^2+2c dv dr+r^2dOmega^2. Radial geodesics use E=f dt/dtau. V_eff=(1-2m/r)(1+l^2/(c^2 r^2)) with V''=2m(r-6m)/(r^3(r-3m)). Kerr in Boyer-Lindquist form with r_pm=m pm sqrt(m^2-a^2) and r_ergo=m+sqrt(m^2-a^2cos^2theta). TOV with the Gamma=2 polytrope p=K rho0^2 integrated in enthalpy. Photon ratio sqrt(f_e/f_r) times local Doppler factors.

strengths: Complete, checkable Schwarzschild derivation, including the Birkhoff staticity step in a details block (R_tr=(2/r) d_t beta).

Correct, careful distinctions: chart failure vs curvature singularity, static-observer divergence vs regular free fall, eternal maximal extension vs collapse spacetime, photon sphere vs image of the horizon.
Kerr uniqueness is qualified with its actual hypotheses and a primary citation (Chrusciel-Costa).

§17.8 TOV is scientifically honest: it states that the toy EOS is not nuclear matter, gives a Newtonian Lane-Emden check and the constant-density benchmark, and says mass-radius turning points need a mode analysis.
The embedded star and photon labs are verified by scripts/check-relativity-models.mjs, and the screenshots show clean controls and readouts.
issues: Kerr is orientation only: no geodesics, Carter constant, spin-dependent ISCO, Penrose process, or 3D ergoregion picture.
No Reissner-Nordstrom solution or inner/Cauchy horizons in this chapter (Cauchy horizons appear only in prose in §22.6).
The manuscript text has no Penrose or Kruskal diagram; the causal map exists only as a separate bridge lesson.
No critical impact parameter (3 sqrt3 m) or shadow calculation, although the text warns against reading images as horizons.
Very dense for a novice: about 3,240 words mixing a derivation, three observer analyses, Kerr, stellar structure and observer redshift in one chapter.
The star lab offers no mass-radius family sweep, so the text's discussion of turning points has nothing to explore.

assets.title: §17.1-17.2 Solving the spherical vacuum equation and testing the horizon with curvature
assets.teaches: How symmetry reduces ten metric functions to two. Which Christoffel symbols matter and why the angular Gamma^r_thetatheta=-r e^(-2beta) term is essential. How G^t_t=(f-1)/r^2+f'/r=0 integrates to f=1-C/r, and how G^r_r minus G^t_t forces alpha+beta constant. How the Newtonian limit fixes C=2GM/c^2. That Birkhoff extends the result to pulsating spherical sources. That K=48m^2/r^6 is finite at 2m and diverges at 0. That horizon tides scale as M^-2 (r_s about 2.95 km per solar mass).
assets.pedagogy: Shows 'a few connection coefficients' and one Ricci component as a mechanism rather than the full list. Explains each term's origin. The integration is presented as the key insight ('explains the inverse-radius form instead of merely announcing it'). The time-dependent case is an optional details block.
assets.physics_model: Static spherical ansatz; mixed Einstein components; the Kretschmann scalar from the six orthonormal curvature entries (-2q,q,q,-q,-q,2q), q=m/r^3.

strengths: The derivation is short enough to follow and complete enough to check.
Explicitly separates the static assumption from Birkhoff's stronger theorem and its non-vacuum limits.
Links back to the Ch. 9 vacuum curvature pattern.

No visual (e.g. an embedding or proper-radial-distance picture) is attached here; the embedding scene is placed after §17.2 by scripts/build-site.mjs sceneSections.

assets.title: §17.3, 17.4 and 17.6 Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, falling vs hovering clocks, and the global event horizon
assets.teaches: The dr^2/f cancellation in v=t+r_*/c. That the horizon block has determinant -c^2 (regular). That outgoing radial light has dr/dv=(c/2)(1-2m/r), so inside even 'outgoing' light moves to smaller r. The conserved energy E=f dt/dtau, the infall rate dr/dtau=-c sqrt(2m/r) and Delta tau=4m/3c from horizon to center. The hovering acceleration GM/(r^2 sqrt(1-2m/r)) diverging at the horizon. Why a distant observer sees redshifted, delayed signals rather than a frozen photograph. And that horizon membership is a global, teleological property, not a local measurement.
assets.pedagogy: Algebraic cancellation shown explicitly. The engine-thrust argument ('can change direction within the cone, cannot produce a direction outside it'). Contrasts two observer families. The eternal-extension vs collapse caveat. The bridge lesson converts slopes to a plot with a dimensionless plotting time, and figure 29 shows tilted cones at r/r_s = 0.5, 1, 1.6, 2.7.
assets.physics_model: ds^2=-f c^2 dv^2+2c dv dr+r^2dOmega^2; radial null directions dv=0 and dr/dv=(c/2)f; timelike radial geodesic with E=1; static four-acceleration a^r=Gamma^r_tt (u^t)^2.

strengths: Conceptually exact treatment of the most misunderstood GR topic, with no escape-speed story.
The comprehensive review singles out horizon teaching as sound: 'Do not replace these with an escape-speed story.'
Figure 29 (horizon-cones) is clean and readable: the outward generator is vertical at r_s and tilted inward inside.
issues: The hovering-acceleration formula needs Gamma^r_tt from §17.1 but the text does not show the magnitude calculation with g_rr.
No interactive light-cone field or infalling-observer animation; the figure is static.
The Kruskal/Penrose material sits in a separate bridge, so the manuscript alone never draws the global causal structure.

assets.title: §17.5 Circular orbits and their stability
assets.teaches: The timelike effective potential with its extra -1/r^3 term. The circular-orbit condition l^2/c^2=mr^2/(r-3m). The stability condition V''>0, giving r>6m. That unstable circular orbits exist between 3m and 6m. That the null potential f/r^2 peaks at the unstable photon sphere r=3m. And how the orbit equation u''+u=GM/l^2+3mu^2 used in Ch. 16 follows by differentiating the energy equation.
assets.pedagogy: Algebraic existence vs stability made explicit ('unstable does not mean algebraically nonexistent'). A summary table of the three radii. A warning that black-hole images are not photographs of r_s. The guides.json check asks whether the three radii coincide.
assets.physics_model: V_eff=(1-2m/r)(1+l^2/(c^2 r^2)); V''=2m(r-6m)/(r^3(r-3m)) at circular orbits; null potential proportional to f/r^2.

strengths: Correct and compact, with the Ch. 16 orbit equation derived rather than assumed.
Good misconception coverage (three radii, photon sphere not a surface).
issues: No plot of V_eff for varying l, which is the canonical visual for this topic.
No orbit integration or precession/zoom-whirl demo.
No critical impact parameter, capture cross-section or shadow size.

assets.title: §17.7 The geometry of a rotating black hole
assets.teaches: The Boyer-Lindquist Kerr metric with Sigma and Delta. The trap in reading g_tphi from the 2g_tphi cross term. That zero angular momentum observers still rotate: dphi/dt=-g_tphi/g_phiphi. The horizon radii r_pm and the ergosurface r_ergo(theta). That the ergoregion means 'cannot stay still' rather than 'cannot escape'. The actual hypotheses behind Kerr uniqueness.
assets.pedagogy: States up front that the metric is taken as given rather than derived. Operational definition of frame dragging. Contrasts inability to stay stationary with inability to escape.
assets.physics_model: Kerr metric in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates, a_K=J/(Mc), |chi|<=1; ZAMO angular velocity; roots of Delta; g_tt=0 surface.

strengths: Correct formulas and a careful uniqueness caveat with a primary citation.

No Kerr geodesics, constants of motion, Carter constant, Penrose process, spin-dependent ISCO or photon orbits.

assets.title: §17.8 A relativistic star has an interior (TOV equation + Stellar structure lab)
assets.teaches: Pressure support needs a gradient, not just pressure. The mass-function metric. How dm/dr and Phi' come from the tt and rr Einstein equations and dp/dr=-(epsilon+p)Phi' from conservation. The three relativistic corrections (pressure inertia, pressure as source, compactness factor) and their Newtonian limit. The integration procedure: regular centre, zero-pressure surface, exterior matching and lapse normalization. A toy Gamma=2 polytrope integrated in enthalpy with series starts. Numerical sensitivity via step halving. The Lane-Emden and constant-density benchmarks. The Buchdahl 8/9 limit with its hypotheses. Why a mass-radius turning point is not by itself a stability proof.
assets.pedagogy: Starts with a slab-of-material picture and a build-outward-from-the-centre narrative before any equation. The lab comes before the derivation so the learner sees profiles first. The prose separates numerical error from EOS uncertainty. The lab prompt: 'watch whether a denser star is also a larger star'.

View toggle: Star (density-shaded disc on fixed reference radius) / Profiles (normalized p, rho, m vs r)

assets.physics_model: Geometric units G=c=K=1. EOS p=rho0^2, epsilon=rho0+p. Enthalpy h=ln(1+2rho0). assets.title: §17.9 Separate the photon from the observers (Light and observers lab)
assets.teaches: Photon frequency is an observer-dependent measurement E=-p.u. Static observers give nu_r/nu_e=sqrt(f_e/f_r). Radial motion at either event multiplies by gamma(1-n beta). The Schwarzschild coordinate travel time c Delta t/r_s=(rho_r-rho_e)+ln((rho_r-1)/(rho_e-1)). A changing coordinate slope does not change the locally measured light speed.
assets.pedagogy: Holds the emission and reception events fixed and varies only the observers. Each graph point is a possible receiver, not a trajectory. The lab shows two wave strips over equal local-time windows so crest counts show frequency directly, plus a 1D radial marker of the two events.

controls: Emission radius r/r_s slider (1.1 to 4, default 2)
Reception radius r/r_s slider (1.1 to 20, default 8)
Emitter velocity / c slider (-0.8 to 0.8; negative is inward)
interaction.what_updates: Recomputes the gravitational and motion factors and redraws the emitted/received wave strips, the event markers on the radial axis, or the frequency-ratio plot.
interaction.rendering: SVG wave strips and plot with no-JS fallback; web/relativity-labs.js enhancement

assets.physics_model: f(r)=1-1/r in units of r_s. gravity=sqrt(f_e/f_r). Doppler (1-n beta)/sqrt(1-beta^2) with n set by propagation direction; ratio = gravity x motion. Checks: 2->8 r_s gives sqrt(4/7), reciprocity of the forward/backward product equals 1, and the pure Doppler case beta=0.6 gives 0.5.

strengths: Clean conceptual separation of photon vs observer, with correct formulas and CI checks.

The wave-strip visual (two strips over equal local-time windows, so crest count is frequency) is novice-friendly; qa/lab-photon-1440-light.png shows 2 r_s to 8 r_s giving 0.75593, which is exactly the CI value sqrt(4/7).
issues: Radial motion only; no transverse or orbital observers, and no light bending or angles.
The radial axis is a 1D line; no spacetime diagram of the null ray between the events.
The travel-time formula is in the text but is not shown as a readout.

The 'Locally measured light speed / c' readout is always 1 by construction; a readout that can never change is a statement, not a measurement, and should become a callout or a comparison with the changing coordinate slope.
